usage: Please pass on a message for me.
Set phrase for relaying spoken words to someone
Fixed greeting; 안부 = 'how someone is doing'
전하다 + 인사/말씀 for delivering a greeting
Common in announcements and the media
examples: 부장님께 이 서류 좀 전해 주세요.
Please hand this document to the manager for me.
Note honorific 께 because the receiver is senior
친구한테 안부 좀 전해 줘.
Tell my friend I said hi.
Casual 한테 + 줘; passing on regards between friends
제 마음을 어떻게 전해야 할지 모르겠어요.
I do not know how to convey how I feel.
전하다 also carries abstract things like feelings
nuance: 전하다 (Sino-Korean 傳, 'transmit/hand down') means relaying something from a sender to a receiver: a message, regards, an item, news, or even a feeling, so the receiver takes 에게/한테 or honorific 께 while the thing passed takes 을/를. The nearest rival is 말하다, but 말하다 is you simply saying something yourself, whereas 전하다 stresses that you are the go-between carrying someone else's words or goods to a third party — '사장님이 잘했다고 전하래요' (the boss told me to tell you 'well done'). Everyday set phrases include 안부를 전하다 (send one's regards), 말씀 전해 주세요 (please pass on the message), and 소식을 전하다 (deliver news). The big English-speaker trap is hearing 전 and thinking 전화하다 ('to make a phone call'): they share the 전 syllable but are unrelated, so '전해 주세요' is 'please relay it', not 'please call them'.

usage: Please let me know the address.
Everyday request for a piece of information
Please let me know in advance.
I let them know the result.
알리다 + 결과/일정/소식 as the thing told
to make known to the world
examples: 도착하면 바로 알려 주세요.
Please let me know as soon as you arrive.
Note 알려 주세요, the form you will use constantly
일정이 바뀌면 미리 알려 줄게요.
If the schedule changes I will let you know in advance.
알려 줄게요 = a promise to inform you
이건 아직 아무한테도 알리지 마세요.
Do not tell anyone about this yet.
알리지 마세요 = please keep it quiet
nuance: 알리다 is the causative of 알다 ('to know'), so literally 'to make (someone) know' — you give a piece of information to a person, who takes 에게/한테, while the fact taught takes 을/를. The form you will reach for ten times a day is 알려 주세요 ('please let me know'), used to ask for an address, a time, a price, or any update. The near-synonym 가르치다 also means 'let know', but 가르치다 leans toward teaching a skill or directions ('역으로 가는 길 좀 가르쳐 주세요'), while 알리다 is just transmitting a fact ('결과를 알려 주세요'). The classic learner error is using plain 알다: 알아요 means 'I know' (a state), and you cannot make a request with it — you must use the causative 알려 주세요 to mean 'inform me'. Beyond person-to-person, 알리다 also covers public announcing — '진실을 세상에 알리다' (reveal the truth to the world).

usage: Do not try to talk me into it.
I barely managed to convince them.
겨우 stresses how hard it was
examples: 팀장님을 설득해서 일정을 바꿨어요.
I persuaded the team lead and changed the schedule.
Result clause shows persuasion succeeded
아무리 설득해도 친구가 안 들어요.
No matter how I try to convince him, my friend will not listen.
아무리 ~해도 = no matter how much
같이 가자고 룸메이트를 설득하는 중이에요.
I am in the middle of convincing my roommate to come along.
~하는 중이에요 = ongoing effort
nuance: 설득하다 (Sino-Korean 說得, literally 'speak-and-gain', i.e. win someone over by talking) means to bring a reluctant person around to your view through reasoning, and crucially the person persuaded takes the object marker 을/를, not 에게 — 친구를 설득하다, never 친구에게 설득하다. Contrast it with 권하다 ('to recommend/urge'): 권하다 is gently offering a suggestion ('커피 한 잔 권하다'), whereas 설득하다 implies active back-and-forth against initial resistance, so it is stronger and more deliberate than just 말하다 or 권하다. The noun 설득 and adjective phrase 설득력이 있다 ('be persuasive') are common. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: because English says 'persuade TO someone' feels wrong but learners still copy 에게 from verbs like 말하다, producing the ungrammatical 사람에게 설득하다. Also note 설득하다 is persuading someone to your side, not convincing yourself — for 'I'm convinced' you would say 납득이 됐어요.

examples: 저녁 약속을 정중하게 거절했어요.
I politely declined the dinner invitation.
Note the polite-softening adverb before the verb
회식을 거절하기가 좀 눈치 보여요.
It feels awkward to turn down the company dinner.
눈치 보이다 = feel socially uncomfortable
부담스러우면 거절해도 돼요.
If it is too much, you can say no.
거절해도 돼요 = giving permission to refuse
nuance: 거절하다 (Sino-Korean 拒絶, 'block-and-sever') is the standard verb for declining a request, offer, or invitation, and the thing refused — 부탁, 제안, 초대 — takes 을/를. Compare it with the harsher 거부하다 (拒否, 'block-and-deny'): 거부하다 is a flat, often institutional rejection ('출석을 거부하다', 'refuse to comply'), while 거절하다 is the ordinary interpersonal 'no thanks'. Because directly refusing can feel rude in Korean social life, 거절하다 is habitually cushioned with 죄송하지만 ('sorry, but…'), 정중하게 ('politely'), or 어렵겠어요 ('that would be difficult'); the bare verb can sound cold. A frequent English-speaker slip is reaching for 거절하다 to mean 'reject a person' romantically — that is 차다 (dump) or 까이다 (get rejected), not 거절하다, which targets the request, not the human. Also do not confuse it with 사양하다, a humble 'I'll pass' used to politely decline an offer of food or a gift.

usage: Please do not scold them too much.
Used when YOU are on the receiving end
크게 혼나다 = get scolded a lot
examples: 선생님이 떠든 학생들을 혼냈어요.
The teacher scolded the noisy students.
Higher-status person disciplining lower
지각했다고 팀장님한테 혼났어요.
I got told off by the team lead for being late.
혼나다 + 한테 marks who scolded you
애를 혼내기 전에 한 번 더 설명해 주세요.
Before you scold the child, please explain once more.
혼내기 전에 = before scolding
nuance: 혼내다 means an older or higher-status person verbally disciplining someone beneath them — a parent a child, a teacher a pupil, a boss a junior — so the person scolded takes 을/를. The essential pair to learn is the active 혼내다 ('I scold') versus 혼나다 ('I get scolded'); '나 혼났어' ('I got chewed out') is something even adults say casually about a partner or boss. Distinguish it from 야단치다 (very close, slightly more old-fashioned/strong, often a parent shouting) and from 화내다, which is just 'to get angry / show anger' with no teaching aim — you can 화내다 at a stranger, but you only 혼내다 someone you have authority over. The English-speaker pitfall is direction: learners say '저는 부장님을 혼났어요' meaning to report being scolded, but that wrongly makes them the scolder; you must flip to 혼나다 — '부장님한테 혼났어요'. Keep 혼내다 (do the scolding) and 혼나다 (receive it) firmly apart.

english: to argue a point / call out
usage: I demanded to know why they did it.
examples: 잘못 계산된 것 같아서 가게에 따졌어요.
It seemed miscalculated so I confronted the shop.
가게에 따지다 = call out the store
사소한 거 가지고 너무 따지지 마세요.
Do not split hairs over such small things.
~가지고 따지다 = quibble about something
조건을 꼼꼼히 따져 보고 계약하세요.
Examine the terms carefully before you sign.
Here 따지다 is calm and analytical
nuance: 따지다 (native Korean, no hanja) has two distinct flavors that share the idea of 'pinning down the truth point by point'. One is confrontational: marching up to someone to demand an explanation for a wrong, where the person/place takes 에게/한테 and the tone is combative — you feel wronged and want answers ('왜 그랬냐고 따졌어'). The other is cool and analytical: scrutinizing or weighing details (조건을 따지다, 가격을 따지다, 손익을 따지다), often with 따져 보다. Compare 물어보다, which is a neutral 'ask a question' with no accusation — switching from 따지다 to 물어보다 instantly removes the hostility. The English-speaker pitfall is using 따지다 for ordinary curiosity: saying '선생님한테 따졌어요' when you merely asked a question sounds like you picked a fight with your teacher; for a polite query use 여쭤봤어요. Read the context to tell the confrontational sense from the analytical one.

usage: Stop being so stubborn about it.
Telling someone to drop the insistence
to insist to the very end
examples: 분명히 틀렸는데 끝까지 우겼어요.
He was clearly wrong but insisted to the end.
분명히 ~인데 sets up the unreasonableness
친구가 자기가 샀다고 우겨서 그냥 졌어요.
My friend insisted on paying so I just gave in.
Common over who pays the bill
증거가 있는데도 안 그랬다고 우기네요.
Even with proof he keeps insisting he did not.
~는데도 = even though; denial despite evidence
nuance: 우기다 (native Korean) means to keep insisting you are right even when you are probably wrong, so it always carries a negative, hard-headed tone — picture someone digging in past the point of reason. It is everyday spoken Korean among friends and family and reports the insistence using ~라고/다고 우기다 ('insist that…'). The key contrast is with the neutral 주장하다 (主張하다, 'to assert/claim'): 주장하다 is dignified and can be perfectly reasonable ('전문가들은 ~라고 주장한다'), whereas 우기다 paints the speaker as obstinate and likely mistaken — you would never use 우기다 in a formal report about your own well-founded position. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 우기다 as a plain synonym for 'insist': in English you can insist correctly and politely, but choosing 우기다 always smuggles in the judgment 'and you're being unreasonable', so for a calm, valid claim switch to 주장하다 or 강조하다.

usage: They are noisy in the classroom.
Place of the racket takes 에서
to be rowdy late at night
examples: 도서관에서는 떠들면 안 돼요.
You must not be noisy in the library.
~면 안 돼요 = it's not allowed
옆 테이블이 너무 떠들어서 시끄러웠어요.
The next table was so loud it was noisy.
~어서 links cause (loud talk) to result
밤늦게 떠들지 마세요. 이웃이 자요.
Do not be loud late at night. The neighbors are sleeping.
Everyday courtesy reminder
nuance: 떠들다 means making a loud, rowdy racket by talking, chattering, or carrying on, and it is almost always framed as something you should NOT do in a quiet place (library, classroom, late at night). Grammatically it is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before ㅂ and ㄴ and ㅅ endings (formal 떠듭니다, command 떠드세요) but stays before a vowel (떠들어요, 떠들었어요) — anchor this on the 요-form 떠들어요, which keeps the ㄹ. Contrast it with the neutral 이야기하다 / 수다 떨다 ('to chat'): 수다 떨다 is friendly gossip with no noise complaint, while 떠들다 specifically flags disruptive volume. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation: by false analogy with regular verbs people write 떠들습니다, but ㄹ drops before ㅂ, giving 떠듭니다; similarly the polite command is 떠드세요, not 떠들세요. Use 떠들다 when volume is the problem, not for ordinary conversation.

usage: to get fooled / I got tricked
examples: 그 사람이 가격을 속여서 비싸게 팔았어요.
He lied about the price and sold it expensive.
가격을 속이다 = misrepresent the price
나이를 속이고 가입하면 안 돼요.
You must not sign up by lying about your age.
속이고 = and (lying about), then…
친구를 속이는 건 정말 나쁜 짓이에요.
Deceiving a friend is a really bad thing to do.
~는 건 nominalizes 'deceiving'
nuance: 속이다 is the causative of 속다 ('to be fooled'), so literally 'to make (someone) be deceived' — to lead a person to believe something false, with the victim taking 을/를 and the falsified fact also often as object (나이를 속이다, 가격을 속이다). The companion verb 속다 / 속았어 ('I got fooled') is just as common in speech, and the two form an essential active/passive pair. Compare 거짓말하다 ('to tell a lie'): 거짓말하다 names the act of uttering a falsehood ('나한테 거짓말했어'), while 속이다 stresses the effect of successfully misleading someone — you can 거짓말하다 and fail, but 속이다 implies the deception landed. The English-speaker pitfall is direction, exactly as with 혼내다: learners say '제가 속였어요' to mean 'I got tricked', but that says you did the tricking; flip to the intransitive — '제가 속았어요' ('I was deceived'). Keep 속이다 (deceive someone) apart from 속다 (be deceived).

Do not blur 속이다 with 거짓말하다: 거짓말하다 is uttering a lie, while 속이다 implies the lie actually misled the victim.

usage: 장난으로 frames it as harmless ribbing
to make fun of someone's looks
examples: 제 사투리를 듣고 친구들이 놀렸어요.
My friends teased me when they heard my dialect.
Teasing over how someone speaks
애를 외모로 놀리면 안 돼요.
You must not make fun of a child's looks.
Note the 'tease about X' particle (으)로
장난으로 놀린 건데 친구가 삐졌어요.
I teased as a joke but my friend got sulky.
삐지다 = sulk; teasing gone wrong
nuance: 놀리다 means making fun of someone, with the target taking 을/를 and the trait teased about taking (으)로 (외모로 놀리다, 사투리로 놀리다). Its emotional range is wide: from affectionate ribbing between close friends to genuinely hurtful mockery, so tone and relationship decide whether it lands as 장난 (a joke) or 상처 (a wound). Watch out for two look-alike traps. First, this 놀리다 (tease) is homonymous with a separate verb 놀리다 meaning 'to leave idle / keep unused' (손을 놀리다 'work the hands', 공장을 놀리다 'idle a factory') — same spelling, unrelated meaning, told apart only by context. Second, English speakers constantly mix 놀리다 (tease) with 놀다 (play, hang out); they share the 놀- root but '친구랑 놀았어요' is 'I hung out with a friend', whereas '친구를 놀렸어요' is 'I teased a friend'. The object particle differs too: 랑/하고 for 놀다 versus 을/를 for 놀리다.

usage: I opened up about my worries.
Feel free to get it off your chest.
to pour out one's true feelings
다 = all of it, holding nothing back
examples: 친한 친구한테 속마음을 털어놨어요.
I confided my true feelings to a close friend.
Listener takes 한테; note contracted 털어놨어요
혼자 끙끙대지 말고 누구한테든 털어놔요.
Do not bottle it up alone; open up to someone.
끙끙대다 = agonize alone
고민이 있으면 언제든 털어놔도 돼요.
If something bothers you, you can confide anytime.
털어놔도 돼요 = it's okay to open up
nuance: 털어놓다 is a compound of 털다 ('to shake/dust out', as you shake out a dusty cloth) plus 놓다 ('to set down'), giving the vivid image of shaking everything out of your chest and laying it on the table — i.e. unburdening worries, secrets, or true feelings you have bottled up, with the listener taking 에게/한테. Because the second element is 놓다, the present and past contract in speech (놓아요 becomes 놔요), giving 털어놔요 and 털어놨어요, while the formal keeps the full stem as 털어놓습니다. Compare 고백하다, which is confessing a specific fact or romantic feeling, whereas 털어놓다 is the broader emotional unburdening of accumulated 고민 to a confidant. The English-speaker pitfall is the contraction: learners over-regularize and write 털어놓았어요 / 털어놓아요, but natural speech is 털어놨어요 / 털어놔요 — and note the imperative drops back to 털어놓으세요 (no contraction before 으). Pair it with 고민, 속마음, 비밀.

usage: I confessed that I like her.
I will be honest and confess.
Owning up to a hidden truth
받다 = be the one confessed to
to work up courage to confess
examples: 용기를 내서 짝사랑하던 사람한테 고백했어요.
I worked up the courage and confessed to my crush.
한테 marks who you confess to; 짝사랑 = one-sided crush
고백했는데 차여서 너무 속상해요.
I confessed but got rejected, so I am really upset.
차이다 = get dumped/rejected
사실 거짓말한 거 고백할게요.
Honestly, I will admit that I lied.
Second sense: owning up to a fault
nuance: 고백하다 (Sino-Korean 告白, literally 'tell-plainly', i.e. lay bare) most often means confessing romantic feelings — '좋아한다고 고백하다' — which in Korean dating culture, especially for people in their 20s-30s, is a defined, weighty moment that frequently marks the official start (사귀다) of a relationship; you 고백하다 first, and if accepted, you are now dating. It also covers admitting a hidden truth or fault, like a heartfelt confession of wrongdoing. The person confessed to takes 에게/한테. Contrast it with 사과하다 ('to apologize', 謝過, expressing regret for a wrong) and with 자백하다 ('to confess to a crime', as to police) — 고백하다 is the warm, personal baring of the heart, not a legal admission or an apology. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'confess' as one word: in English you 'confess your love' and 'confess to the crime' alike, but Korean reserves 고백하다 for heartfelt romantic/personal disclosure and uses 자백하다 for criminal confession; choosing 고백하다 with the police sounds oddly intimate.
